To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

dietary vitamin A deficiency in chickens is characterized by a decrease in plasma vitamin A concentration and by an increase in plasma ascorbic acid concentration, and that these changes can be prevented by the administration of vitamin A or ascorbic acid.
dietary vitamin A and AA interact synergistically to improve growth performance and immune function in broiler chickens.
dietary AA supplementation to the vitamin A-deficient chick is able to prevent the occurrence of scurvy-like symptoms and to increase liver vitamin A stores.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effect of AA on the vitamin A deficiency in chickens.
the effects of dietary AA on vitamin A deficiency, and with the effect of dietary AA on liver stores of vitamin A. MATERIAL
the effect of AA on the vitamin A deficiency syndrome in chicks.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
AA supplementations to the chick diets have a beneficial effect on vitamin A deficiency.
dietary ascorbic Acid (AA) supplementation to chicks on a low vitamin A diet, did not affect their vitamin A status, as measured by liver stores of the vitamin.

the AA supplementations to the vitamin A deficient chicks did not affect the growth and feed consumption, but the vitamin A supplementations to the chicks fed a diet containing adequate amounts of AA, increased the growth rate and feed consumption.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
AA supplementations to chicks fed vitamin A deficient diets, resulted in a significant improvement of the growth rate, the feed conversion and the vitamin A reserves in the liver.
the addition of ascorbic acid to a vitamin A-deficient diet did not cure the vitamin A deficiency, but it improved the growth and feed efficiency and increased the vitamin A content of the liver.
the administration of AA to vitamin A deficient chicks is not beneficial, but rather harmful, since it increases vitamin A requirements.
The main takeaway from our work is that
vitamin A is a critical nutrient for maintaining a strong immune system and that vitamin A deficiency may be a risk factor for severe COVID-19.
the effects of ascorbic acid are complex and not fully understood.
ascorbic acid is not a vitamin for chickens, and the addition of ascorbic acid to poultry diets does not prevent the symptoms of vitamin A deficiency.
